doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Work, pay and the New York life
title: Getting visa and citizenship; the value of travel
summary: The easier 1994 scene, a club-date sponsor and 01 visa, the citizenship paperwork about travel history, and how travel changes her perspective.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Have you noticed that it’s gotten harder in your 22 years?

Yes. Because even when I first came here and I was doing gigs on Broadway, there was still a happening studio scene in New York. There were still things going on. I mean I think that time in New York was really great. I got hooked up with a whole corporate party scene at the end of ’94, and I got sponsored by this club date organization, you know, sponsored for an 01 visa. So I was actually able to get legal. This would be much harder to do, I mean what I did then, now. It’s a different time in a post 9/11 world and the politics are much different now, and you know it was a much easier time then. You know there were all these gigs and corporate, and all that, and so I got sponsored for an 01 visa. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

01 artist visa for three years. So I had a sponsor and I worked with her on and off for the next three years, and started paying taxes and got a Social Security card. So within six months of being here I was a legal resident.

No I am not. In fact this week I have to go and renew my green card, and then citizenship. I want to be a citizen by this time next year, so I’ll let you know if I’ve crossed that hurdle. It’s a lot of paperwork. And the hardest question for me is two questions on the citizenship paper that are very hard for musicians, namely your employers, and namely where you’ve been since the green card. So if not five years, if not ten years, well where have you been outside the country. Well I did so many one- nighters I don’t even remember. I’ve got two passports to go through, you know, it’s like wow. So there’s a couple of questions that aren’t really geared for us. All they really want to know is were you in the Middle East at all. That’s what they want to know. But they have to know exactly where you’ve been. Maybe you were in Pakistan. Maybe you were in places that are on the watch. So it’s very hard. The process is going to take me a lot of time to go through. Daunting for someone who’s not tip-top organized.
Wow. I mean do you save you calendars from year to year?

Yeah I’ve got my calendars saved. But sometimes I would write, literally, when I was doing a lot of traveling — “Europe” — “Back from Europe” and that would be like three weeks. What was I doing those three weeks. Honestly I don’t even know what country I was in sometimes if I went from Warsaw to Czechoslovakia. I might not even have written, I might have been asleep the whole time and not written in my book.
Oh that’s funny. I just was talking to another musician about that fact, that like people think that your travel is so great because you get to go to all these places.

It is. It’s one of the perks. And I never forget that. When I meet people that haven’t been out of the country. And you’re like ten years older than me and you’ve been once to Europe? Oh, you’ve got to go back. And you’ve got to go to this place. And I feel for them in a way. You know what I mean? Not that — there’s so many beautiful places to go in America of course, it’s a wonderful place to be, of course. But you need a comparison point. And every time I go back to Europe and come back I have a different perspective. I cook differently. I live a little differently. You know what I mean? And then I have a different perspective on now I’m on the outside looking in. And I don’t know I just feel it’s when we cook, it really is. It’s hard work, but it’s so good. Absolutely. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
